Hello!
Please tell me, why doesn't Lean use Homotopy Type Theory? It's very powerful and interesting.
Although I heard somewhere that an even more interesting and powerful one, HOTT, is being developed. I don't remember the translation. I think "O" stands for "observable."
#Type theory

According to #leantt, HoTT is inconsistent with uniqueness of proofs.
I think proof irrelevance makes Lean more convenient, although Rocq doesn't include it by default and seems to be fine.

Funny enough, Lean 2 did have a HoTT version if I remember correctly. But I think Lean 3 chose to specialize to non-HoTT math, and Lean 4 chose to specialize even further to classical math (and you will have a lot of trouble doing constructive math in Lean 4). I believe these were practical decisions to support and optimize for the most common use cases. And as @Snir Broshi just said, some features of Lean are incompatible with HoTT (although there are workarounds for those willing to try).

Jason Rute said:

(and you will have a lot of trouble doing constructive math in Lean 4).

I suspect you meant to say doing intuitionistic math is hard in lean 4, right?
As in, many lean tactics are happy to use choice, even if it might not be strictly needed?

Edward van de Meent said:

I suspect you meant to say doing intuitionistic math is hard in lean 4, right?

What distinction are you drawing here? 'Constructive' and 'intuitionistic' are often synonyms.

Sometimes the two are not synonyms. There are those who will happily use LEM in their constructions of things, and consider the result explicit and constructive. Of course, such as those are unlikely to spend time considering intuitionism.

content:
James E Hanson said:

Edward van de Meent said:

I suspect you meant to say doing intuitionistic math is hard in lean 4, right?

What distinction are you drawing here? 'Constructive' and 'intuitionistic' are often synonyms.

Ah, reading back now I realise my mistake, I misread your message :see_no_evil: it was late, and both "constructive" and "classical" start with C

FWIW, although Lean 4 doesn't have direct support for HoTT at the kernel level, it's possible to build a HoTT "layer" on top. @Sina Hazratpour spoke about this at the Swiss Math Soc formalization meeting last week, maybe he can comment more.

I'm not completely sure of the circumstances surrounding this decision, but I think there were a combination of technical and nontechnical reasons to avoid HoTT.

On the technical side, HoTT would require giving up

  • Definitional proof irrelevance, where p = q holds by definition if p q : P and P : Prop. Note that HoTT can actually support non-definitional proof irrelevance via something known as propositional truncation (the Lean equivalent are docs#Squash and docs#Trunc).
  • Subsingleton elimination. My understanding is that the real issue is the existence of the impredicative Prop universe which has different universe rules, although someone more knowledgeable could probably comment on this.
  • We would have to downgrade from the axiom of global choice that exists in mathlib to the regular axiom of choice.

Additionally, with the way mathlib is set up, the benefits of HoTT are somewhat diminished:

  • In HoTT, the univalance axiom makes it so that Int = Nat is not a proposition but rather the type of bijections between Int and Nat, and that A = B where A B : CategoryTheory.Bundled Group is the type of group isomorhpisms between A and B. In Mathlib, we avoid = when referring to things with types so the benefits are diminished. Additionally, CategoryTheory.Bundled is hardly used because Lean prefers to rely on the typeclass system.
  • The real advantage of the univalance axiom is not just that you get to use the prettier looking = symbol rather than ≃ when referring to types, but that you can transport properties of types across equalities. In particular, the only functions f : CategoryTheory.Bundled Group -> Prop that HoTT lets you define must respect group isomorphism, so then you get that A = B -> f A = f B. For example, if f A were the statement that A is abelian, then HoTT lets you conclude for free that any group isomorphic to an abelian group is abelian. But in Mathlib, we often actually want the stronger statement that if B is a group and there is a surjective homomorphism h : A -> B, then B is abelian. HoTT does not help with this theorem and we need it in mathlib, but it implies the statement that HoTT gives us for free. See #maths > Carneiro's thesis (transfer tactic not needed)

On the nontechnical side, there are a few reasons:

  • The one that gets talked about a lot is that Lean is optimized for classical mathematics, while many of the same people that work on HoTT prefer intuitionistic math. I'm pretty sure HoTT can be used classically so this not a technical barrier. Rather, the worry is that HoTT researchers would not actually be fully satisfied if Lean were to add HoTT.
  • HoTT is a very active area of research and there's still too much that is not known about the metatheory of HoTT. There are many different versions of HoTT, including book HoTT, cubical type theory, HOTT (as you mentioned, though I've not heard of this), etc. Many of these are axiomatically quite complicated, and cubical type theory has tons of primitives. If Lean were to adopt one of these, which one would be the best? Lean needs to pick a type theory and commit permanently to it; it can't afford to pick an experimental type theory.
  • Adding HoTT makes Lean harder to learn.

I think a lot of the appeal of Lean is that its type theory is not very intrusive. Once you learn the standard translations like set to type or ∈ to : most things just kind of work. Sure, sometimes you run against universe issues, sometimes you have to deal with a bunch of casts, but these annoyances often point to actual subtleties in the mathematics, such as the distinction between sets and classes, or the fact that some isomorphism isn't actually the identity function. I don't think the same can be said for "equality is now data".
It is worth noting that in HoTT, many types like Nat and Int are classified as "sets" which means that equality within them is no longer data. But equality between elements of Type is very much data.

Niels Voss said:

  • I'm pretty sure HoTT can be used classically so this not a technical barrier.

IIRC, one can have LEM for many sets (i.e. types of h-level=2), just not for types generally. In any case, you can establish decidable equality for specific sets of interest, and then classical reasoning about them is fine. (Disclaimer: I'm not an expert on HoTT, just an interested long-term bystander)

There is also a conceptual issue with code generation if Lean does not have proof irrelevance. In the generated C code proofs, including proof fields of a structure, are erased. So the C code cannot depend on proofs. In the absence of proof irrelevance it is not clear to me what it would even mean to say that the C code is correct.

That’s not an issue with HoTT embeddings inside lean anyway. Further if lean itself would have hypothetically use HoTT as the title of this thread suggests then proof erasure would probably not be a thing or maybe follow a different strategy
How? I mean if we have a function f: Fin 3 -> Bool so that f(<n, p>) depended on the specific proof p : n < 3, then what code can we generate?
When running that program you would not have those dependent types in the first place
It would be compiled down to f : Nat -> Bool
This is true for any dependently typed language
You did not answer the question. The point is that if it depends on p then it is not well-defined as a function f: Nat -> Bool. So "compiled down" makes no sense.

You are missing my point. When compiling, you just erase those dependent types after type checking. For HoTT, the type theory itself has a no erasure principles. The complicated answer in cubical agda appears to be marking certain types for erasure (resource : https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~nad/publications/abel-danielsson-vezzosi-erased-univalence.pdf)
Will someone with actual understanding please tell me if my point is correct or not.

My point is that if we have a function f: Fin n -> Bool this does not induce a well-defined function f: Nat -> Bool unless one has proof irrelevance. Proof irrelevance in this case is exactly that we have a well-defined function from {0, 1, 2} -> Bool, which can be then extended to Nat.

If f (<1, p>) and f (<1, q>) are different for two proofs p, q : 1 < 3, then which of the values should we take for f (1) when we pass to natural numbers.

I have thought through this and understood this as an issue which requires proof irrelevance. Am I missing something?
the compiler transforms your function into one which isn't well defined according to the type theory

I think you don't get proof irrelevance in general, but you can prove it on some types. For instance, it's true on Nat. So a function on Fin n does lift (because proofs are irrelevant there) but that's a theorem.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

If f (<1, p>) and f (<1, q>) are different for two proofs p, q : 1 < 3, then which of the values should we take for f (1) when we pass to natural numbers.

At runtime you just get 1 and a guarantee that 1 < n is inhabited

Thanks @Aaron Liu - would that not be considered seriously undesirable behaviour? We want the compiled code to be well-defined and the same as running witing.

Thansk @Sébastien Gouëzel - that is a very good point. I take it you mean a theorem in HoTT.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

Thanks Aaron Liu - would that not be considered seriously undesirable behaviour? We want the compiled code to be well-defined and the same as running witing.

It turns out to be fine because for example if we're lifting a Fin n -> Nat we make sure to only input Nats which are < n, in which case the compiler makes sure the compiled function will do the same thing (and running it with something not < n is undefined behavior)
For my case Fin n was an example. Suppose we took a type where we have more than one proof, say equality with Bool -> Bool. Would this not make things dubious?
At @Aaron Liu the issue is not numbers bigger than 3. See my example. The issue is f 1 can have two possible candidate values
Just to clarify, there are dependently typed languages that don't have a proof irrelevant Prop type that have dependent type erasure. Dependent types are used to type check and compiled away.
Not literally in this case due to the argument of @Sébastien Gouëzel but in general.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

At Aaron Liu the issue is not numbers bigger than 3. See my example. The issue is f 1 can have two possible candidate values

It's not possible to write a well-typed function in Lean that gives different values depending on what proof you give it.
Aaron, we're talking about HoTT here.
In Lean, yes. But if Lean did not have proof erasure then it would be I believe.
If Lean did not have proof erasure then everything is fine probably?
Sorry, I mistyped. I meant if we do not have proof irrelevance but do have proof erasure, we will have logical inconsistencies
if we have proof erasure but not proof irrelevance then compiling functions becomes very difficult
My point. I mean not just difficult but with some real logical issues.

So to get back to what I was trying to say in response to the original question: Why doesn't Lean have HoTT? One factor could be:

  • Since Lean programs run and fast, we need proof erasure.
  • Proof erasure without proof irrelevance is logically unsound.
  • Hence we cannot have HoTT.

What does running fast have anything to do with proof erasure? Rocq extracts to ocaml which can in principle run efficiently (upto rocq extraction to ocaml and ocaml compiler limits). Rocq does not have definitional proof irrelevance.

@Shreyas Srinivas if you can answer my precise mathematical question (what should f (1) be, or why this is not an issue) please do so. I am ready to understand. Random comments that someone has solved something somehow do not help.

I am trying to understand your question. You are saying we need proof irrelevance to extract running code (efficiently?) in dependently typed languages. Yet there are many languages that do not have proof irrelevance and manage to extract code anyway (albeit with human annotations like in Agda or Idris)
Definitional proof irrelevance is also something we want, how would this work with HoTT?

@Siddhartha Gadgil : A concrete example of f would be helpful to me to understand your question. Otherwise I find this question too broad, and the answer is : there are many ways to get (sound?) erasure in specific scenarios and it's complicated.
@Aaron Liu it doesn't. The whole point of HoTT is the rich structure of proofs (becoming the loop space), which gets killed by proof irrelevance.
Siddhartha : But you are right about one thing, HoTT (standard book presentation) itself has no type erasure rules.

Let me try a concrete case.

In HoTT there are two different proofs that Bool = Bool, corresponding to the isomorphisms hence equalities that not and identity. These are not equal. We consider a structure X with two fields - a Bool and an equality f : Bool -> Bool. I define a function f: X -> Bool mapping <x, p> to p x, where we think of p as a function.

Then we get f (<true, id>) = true but f(<true, not>) = false. If we now try to erase the proof, we should get a function f : Bool -> Bool. But f (true) will have to be both true and false, or rather we do not have a well-defined quotient.

To use some lean style jargon, in HoTT, id and not would be considered data and not erased. Fwiw you can also write this example in (obviously non-HoTT) lean:

import Mathlib

structure ExampleProd where
  val : Bool
  eq : Equiv Bool Bool
deriving BEq

instance : Repr (ExampleProd) where
  reprPrec x _ := repr x.val


def idBool : Equiv Bool Bool where
  toFun := id
  invFun := id

def notBool : Equiv Bool Bool where
  toFun := not
  invFun := not
  left_inv := by
    simp [Function.LeftInverse]
  right_inv := by
    simp [Function.RightInverse, Function.LeftInverse]

def ex1 : ExampleProd := ⟨true, idBool⟩

def ex2 : ExampleProd := ⟨true, notBool⟩

def f : ExampleProd → Bool := fun v => v.val

#eval f ex1

#eval f ex2

#eval ex1 == ex2

#eval (f ex1 == f ex2)

What I mean is f in the following:

  invFun := id

This does not induce a function f : Bool -> Bool as f true is problematic.
Yes you are correct. I don't see why you believe we can't get running code here though? In the HoTT world, id and not are data. You can condition and "pattern match" on them.
This puzzled me a bit but I see that Equiv Bool Bool is a Type, not a Prop. Otherwise Lean would have prevented me from defining f in that way.
I think I am beginning to see why you say we can't extract running code.
Please let me try responding

I'll try to construct examples, but the gist is: you can actually use proof in HoTT as data objects. You can "pattern match" (I am still wrapping my head around HIITs) and condition on them. In Lean proofs are irrelevant, so computable functions cannot depend on proofs.
That was my point. We need proofs to be irrelevant to ensure that computable functions cannot depend on proofs. This is a reason not to have HoTT in Lean.
By reason I mean merely tradeoff, i.e., this would be a cost to having HoTT in Lean.
And my confusion with your question is: I understood your question to mean we can't extract computable (or efficient) code from HoTT (well cubical TT at least).
I meant only that one specific optimisation used by Lean is blocked by HoTT. I don't know how much it matters.

Let's just say proof erasure without proof irrelevance is non trivial. In Agda you have two kinds of irrelevance annotations : compile-time and runtime (see more here and here). You tag types with the correct erasure modality and the compiler checks that it can actually erase that information by checking that the underlying function doesn't depend on the annotated type.

I like Agda a lot, but Agda programs don't actually run. The only comparable language I know is Idris. I don't know what happens there.

But coming to the example, if we replaced equivalence by "existence of equivalence", which is a Prop, then Lean does block the definition of f.

import Mathlib

structure ExampleProd where
  val : Bool
  eq : Nonempty (Equiv Bool Bool)
deriving BEq

instance : Repr (ExampleProd) where
  reprPrec x _ := repr x.val


def idBool : Equiv Bool Bool where
  toFun := id
  invFun := id

def notBool : Equiv Bool Bool where
  toFun := not
  invFun := not
  left_inv := by
    simp [Function.LeftInverse]
  right_inv := by
    simp [Function.RightInverse, Function.LeftInverse]

def ex1 : ExampleProd := ⟨true, Nonempty.intro idBool⟩

def ex2 : ExampleProd := ⟨true, Nonempty.intro notBool⟩

/--
error: Tactic `cases` failed with a nested error:
Tactic `induction` failed: recursor `Nonempty.casesOn` can only eliminate into `Prop`

motive : Nonempty (Bool ≃ Bool) → Sort ?u.1150
h_1 : (f : Bool ≃ Bool) → motive ⋯
x✝ : Nonempty (Bool ≃ Bool)
⊢ motive x✝ after processing
  _
the dependent pattern matcher can solve the following kinds of equations
- <var> = <term> and <term> = <var>
- <term> = <term> where the terms are definitionally equal
- <constructor> = <constructor>, examples: List.cons x xs = List.cons y ys, and List.cons x xs = List.nil
-/
#guard_msgs in
def f : ExampleProd → Bool := fun v =>
  match v.eq with
  | Nonempty.intro f =>
    f (v.val)

Yes you can't pattern match on proofs of a Lean Prop since all proofs of a prop are identical. This is not necessarily true in other dependently typed languages. Lean inductive Props don't have the noConfusion property. The Hitchhiker's guide to logical verification briefly mentions this.

@Siddhartha: to add to all the above, and in response to the efficiency issue you point out, a lot of “efficient” code in lean tends to be unsafe anyway. Code about which proofs can be easily written is usually less efficient. For example a lean array code uses implemented_by’ and unsafe` to achieve efficiency and is relatively harder/impossible to reason about than, say, the same code using lists.
